clue.text: Bill gets free bitter

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill to be settled
to rid is to free or clear

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill is let off and feels resentful about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but here it is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a sharp, harsh taste or smell, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Where you can see washing at every point

definitions.meaning: laundry hangs out to dry pegged on a cord

explanation.definitionFit: Laundry is pegged on a clothes line, and the idiom means completely or everywhere.

clue.text: Restore Frenchman to wife

parts.note: René is a typical French man's name

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is reunited with his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something like new again is to restore it.

clue.text: Annoyance expressed by "Hell and "Blast"

parts.note: Dis is the classical underworld, a name for hell
a gust is a blast of wind

explanation.surface: Someone shows irritation by swearing 'Hell!' and 'Blast!'.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like oaths, but they are the underworld and a wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong distaste or indignation is a form of annoyance.

clue.text: Supporter concealing piece of malicious chatter

indicators.note: the supporter's word hides the piece inside itself, so one sits within the other

parts.note: a backer supports a cause or venture
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: A loyal ally is secretly hiding a scrap of spiteful gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'malicious chatter' reads as gossip itself, but it is the person who chatters maliciously.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who speaks spitefully of people behind their backs is one who chatters with malice.

clue.text: Gathering to cook

definitions.meaning: a gathering is a swelling full of pus, an abscess

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a pus-filled skin swelling and heating food in water.

clue.text: Jack Sprat wouldn't indulge in gossip

definitions.meaning: the nursery rhyme says Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so he would not munch any

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to chat at leisure, and literally Jack Sprat refused to eat fat.

clue.text: Rustic with a lot of objection to pain

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: but is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'
colic is a sharp abdominal pain

explanation.surface: A countryman makes a fuss about stomach ache.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe country life, pastoral and rural.

clue.text: Having bother getting up, one's brought before Head for unpunctuality

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the word rises, so it is read bottom to top

parts.note: drat is a mild oath like bother
I is the Roman numeral one
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A pupil who struggles to get up in the morning is sent to the headteacher for being late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting up' turns DRAT into TARD. 'Head' looks like a headteacher but is a promontory.
explanation.definitionFit: Lateness is a failure to be on time, the opposite of punctuality.

clue.text: Fairy's dressing of wool led to change

parts.note: robing is putting on robes, dressing

indicators.note: the letters are made to change their order

explanation.surface: A fairy's outfit made of wool needed altering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges OF WOOL LED into OODFELLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: This mischievous sprite of English folklore, also called Puck, is a fairy.

clue.text: Revolutionary led island to overwhelming victory

indicators.note: something revolutionary overturns things, so these letters are turned over into a new order

explanation.surface: A rebel leads an island to a crushing win in a war of independence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a rebel leader, but it signals rearranging LED ISLAND.
explanation.definitionFit: An election won by a huge margin is called by this word, borrowed from a collapsing hillside.

clue.text: Substitute chocaholics are really outraged by, initially?

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each of the five words before it

explanation.surface: Chocolate lovers are scandalised by a replacement for their favourite food.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what chocolate fans hate; the first letters of five words give it.
explanation.definitionFit: Powder from the pods of this tree is widely used as a chocolate replacement, so it is a substitute.

clue.text: It's allowable, but shocking, when laid on the line

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece laid on another is written after it

parts.note: L is the usual abbreviation for line
awful means shocking or terrible

explanation.surface: Something is permitted, yet appalling, when stated bluntly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid on the line' sounds like the idiom for speaking frankly, but it places AWFUL after L.
explanation.definitionFit: What the law permits is legal and therefore allowed, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Stable with one acceptable horse

parts.note: a stall is a compartment in a stable
I is the Roman numeral for one
on is used colloquially for acceptable, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: A stable has room for a single horse that is good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like the horse's home in the picture; it gives the stall.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an uncastrated male horse, kept especially for breeding.

clue.text: Without regard to the consequences, like Charles II

definitions.meaning: going at something recklessly, with no care for the outcome
Charles the Bald was Charles II of France and Holy Roman Emperor

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means rushing in recklessly, and the Frankish king Charles II was nicknamed 'the Bald'.

clue.text: A number impair efficiency of probation

parts.note: NO is the abbreviation of number
to vitiate is to spoil or make less effective

explanation.surface: A few people undermine the working of a trial period at work.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice's trial period in a religious order is a probation before taking vows.

clue.text: Adaptable relatives adapted

indicators.note: adapted means altered, so the letters of relatives are reworked

explanation.surface: Family members prove flexible by adjusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flexible who can turn to many tasks is adaptable.

clue.text: Belief in sacred objects

indicators.note: in shows the answer is tucked inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Faith resides in holy relics.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed or statement of faith is a set of beliefs, named from Latin 'I believe'.

clue.text: Seaman returning to deck, sort of

parts.note: tar is old slang for a sailor

indicators.note: returning means the little word to is read backwards

explanation.surface: A sailor goes back to swabbing the ship's deck, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deck' looks like a ship's deck beside the sailor, but it is a deck of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a pack of cards used for fortune-telling, so a deck of a special kind.

clue.text: Victory (with valuable card I held) over Henry

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above, so this comes first
held means the card holds the letter inside it

parts.note: a trump is a card of the suit that beats all others
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A card player wins by holding a trump and beating someone called Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' looks like a rival player but is the electrical unit symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A great success or win is a victory.

clue.text: Identified tune with help, backing by newspaperman

indicators.note: backing tells us the tune and help are turned round together, each read back to front

parts.note: a song is a tune
aid means help
ED, short for editor, is a newspaperman

explanation.surface: A journalist recognises a melody that comes with a supporting backing track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns SONGAID into DIAGNOS, which comes before ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors determine a patient's illness from symptoms, so this means identified the condition.

clue.text: He may hold shares in pit, in one that's fraudulent

indicators.note: in puts the pit inside the rearranged letters
fraudulent means false or crooked, so the word one is twisted out of shape

parts.note: a mine is a pit

explanation.surface: A shareholder in a coal pit turns out to be a swindler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's fraudulent' reshuffles the word one into NOE; the surface makes the shareholder the crook, but fraudulent only signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A person named to hold shares on behalf of the true owner is so called.

clue.text: Someone questioned when an explosive device is found in river

indicators.note: is found in places the device inside the name of the river

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, England
a mine is an explosive device

explanation.surface: A suspect is interrogated after a bomb turns up in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate sitting a test is a person being asked questions.

clue.text: One leaves home before catching plane

indicators.note: catching means one word holds the other within it

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
a MiG is a Russian fighter plane

explanation.surface: Someone departs from the house just before boarding a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a traveller with a flight to catch; ERE is the thing doing the catching.
explanation.definitionFit: An emigrant, especially a political exile, has left their native country.

clue.text: Beaver skin after completion of dressing

indicators.note: after places the piece that follows ahead of this one
completion of points to the last letter of the word dressing

parts.note: rind is the tough skin of fruit or cheese

explanation.surface: An animal's pelt is ready once the dressing has been finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beaver' looks like the animal whose skin is dressed; it is the verb meaning to work hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To beaver away is to toil steadily, which is to slog or labour hard.

clue.text: Almost lower boat

indicators.note: almost means the word falls just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: to lower (rhyming with 'flower') is to frown, to scowl

explanation.surface: Nearly drop a small vessel down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' looks like 'let down' but is the verb meaning to frown.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a flat-bottomed boat used for carrying cargo.

clue.text: I had quickly found island, in a manner of speaking

parts.note: I had said quickly is contracted to I'd
IOM is the abbreviation of the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of having found an island fast, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quickly' looks like part of the story, but it signals the contraction of 'I had'.
explanation.definitionFit: A characteristic expression or turn of phrase is a way of putting things in language.

clue.text: Celandine flourished every so many years

indicators.note: flourished suggests something waved about and rearranged, so the flower's letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A celandine bloomed only once in a long while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flourished' is a natural verb for a flower, which hides its job as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Happening once every ten years is happening at a fixed interval of years.

clue.text: Observes way in which advertisement's introduced make-up

parts.note: eyes as a verb means observes or watches

indicators.note: introduced means one piece is put into the middle of another

parts.note: how means the way in which
ad is short for advertisement

explanation.surface: Someone watches how a cosmetics advert is launched.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cosmetic applied to the eyelids, one type of make-up.

clue.text: Both 24 and 27 do make a presentation

parts.note: the two answers referred to both finish with the same pair of letters, O and W, so the phrase reads as what they do at their close

explanation.surface: Two earlier entries each hand over a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'both end OW': the two referenced answers each finish in those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestow a gift or fund on someone is to make a presentation of it.
